stem: Which definition of economics describes it as the science of human behaviour as a relationship between ends and scarce means that have alternative uses?
explanation: Robbins built his definition on unlimited ends, scarce means and alternative uses of those means. Marshall's definition stresses material welfare, and Smith's calls economics the science of wealth.

stem: The basic economic problem that every society faces arises because
options: wants are unlimited while resources are scarce
governments collect too much in taxes
money and income are unevenly shared among people
prices tend to rise over time
explanation: Scarcity of resources relative to unlimited wants forces every society to choose what, how and for whom to produce. Unequal incomes and inflation are problems in some economies, but they are not the root of the basic problem.

stem: Bilal can spend his Saturday either working at a shop for Rs 2,000 or attending a coaching class. He chooses the class. What is the opportunity cost of the class?
options: Nothing, as he chose the class freely
The fee he pays for the class
The value of the knowledge he gains
explanation: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative forgone, here the Rs 2,000 wage. The knowledge gained is the benefit of the class, not its cost.

stem: A production possibility curve that is concave (bowed outward) from the origin shows that
options: opportunity cost falls as more of one good is produced
opportunity cost rises as more of one good is produced
opportunity cost stays constant along the curve
explanation: Resources are not equally suited to both goods, so each extra unit of one good costs more and more of the other: increasing opportunity cost gives the outward bow. A straight-line PPC would show constant cost.

stem: An economy is producing at a point inside its production possibility curve. This means that
options: the economy is producing beyond its full productive capacity
some resources are unemployed or used inefficiently
explanation: Points on the curve use all resources fully and efficiently; a point inside it means output could rise without giving anything up. Points outside the curve are unattainable with current resources.

stem: An outward shift of the whole production possibility curve is most likely caused by
options: a fall in the price of one good
a move from unemployment to full employment
explanation: Better technology or more resources increase the economy's capacity to produce both goods, shifting the curve outward. Reducing unemployment moves the economy from inside the curve to the curve, not the curve itself.

stem: Which branch of economics studies the behaviour of an individual firm or household?
explanation: Microeconomics studies individual units such as a consumer, firm or industry. Macroeconomics deals with aggregates such as national income and the general price level.

stem: Which statement is a normative statement?
options: Higher interest rates can reduce borrowing by firms and households
Pakistan imports some of its crude oil
A rise in price reduces the quantity demanded
The government ought to reduce the tax on wheat
explanation: A normative statement is a value judgement about what ought to be and cannot be tested by facts. The others are positive statements that can be checked against evidence.

stem: According to the law of demand, other things remaining the same,
options: quantity demanded rises when income rises
quantity demanded falls when price rises
explanation: The law of demand states an inverse relation between a good's own price and the quantity demanded, ceteris paribus. The income effect describes a shift of demand, not the law of demand itself.

stem: The price of tea rises. Which of the following is most likely to happen in the market for sugar, a good used with tea?
options: Demand for sugar falls and its curve shifts left
The supply curve of sugar shifts right
Demand for sugar rises and its curve shifts right
Quantity of sugar demanded rises along its curve
explanation: Tea and sugar are complements: dearer tea means less tea drunk and so less sugar wanted at every price, shifting sugar's demand curve left. A movement along the curve would need a change in sugar's own price.

stem: A movement along a demand curve, rather than a shift of the curve, is caused by a change in
options: the price of the good itself
the price of a substitute good
explanation: Only a change in the good's own price moves the consumer along a given demand curve. Income, prices of related goods and tastes are the conditions of demand: they shift the whole curve.

stem: Ayesha's income rises and she buys less of a cheap brand of cooking oil. For her, this oil is
options: a Giffen good with an upward demand curve
explanation: An inferior good is one whose demand falls as income rises, because buyers switch to better alternatives. A normal good's demand rises with income, and a Giffen good is a rare inferior good whose demand rises with its own price.

stem: A Giffen good is an exception to the law of demand because, when its price rises,
options: its supply rises at the same time
buyers expect its price to rise even further in the coming months
it is bought to show off wealth
a strong negative income effect outweighs the substitution effect
explanation: For a staple inferior good taking a large share of a poor household's budget, a price rise cuts real income so much that the family buys more of the staple and less of better food. Buying to show off wealth describes a Veblen good, a different exception.

stem: Expensive diamonds being bought more when their price rises, because they signal status, is an example of
explanation: Veblen goods are demanded partly for their high price as a status symbol, so demand can rise with price. A Giffen good is an inferior staple, not a luxury.

stem: Which of the following shifts the supply curve of wheat to the right?
options: A new tax on each bag of wheat
A rise in the price of wheat
A fall in the price of fertiliser
A rise in consumers' incomes and spending on bread
explanation: Cheaper inputs lower the cost of production, so farmers offer more wheat at every price. A rise in wheat's own price causes a movement along the supply curve, and a tax per unit shifts supply left.

stem: The law of supply states that, other things being equal,
options: quantity supplied rises as price rises
quantity supplied rises as price falls
explanation: Higher prices make production more profitable and draw in more output, so price and quantity supplied move in the same direction. The equality of supply and demand describes equilibrium, not the law of supply.

stem: In a market, the quantity demanded is greater than the quantity supplied at the current price. What will happen next if the market is free?
options: Price will rise until the shortage disappears
Price will fall until the excess supply disappears
Supply curve will shift to the left
explanation: Excess demand is a shortage: buyers compete for scarce goods and bid the price up, which lowers quantity demanded and raises quantity supplied until they are equal. A surplus would push the price down instead.

stem: The demand for a good is Qd = 100 − 4P and the supply is Qs = 20 + 4P. What is the equilibrium price?
explanation: Set 100 − 4P = 20 + 4P, so 80 = 8P and P = 10. The equilibrium quantity is 100 − 40 = 60 units. Rs 20 comes from dividing 80 by 4 instead of 8.

stem: Demand for a good is Qd = 120 − 2P and supply is Qs = 3P − 30. If the government fixes a maximum price of Rs 25, the market will have
options: neither a shortage nor a surplus
explanation: Equilibrium is where 120 − 2P = 3P − 30, so P = 30. The ceiling of Rs 25 is below it: Qd = 120 − 50 = 70 and Qs = 75 − 30 = 45, a shortage of 70 − 45 = 25 units. 45 is the quantity supplied, not the gap.

stem: If both demand and supply of a good increase by the same amount, the equilibrium
options: price rises while quantity stays the same
quantity rises while price stays about the same
explanation: A rightward shift of demand raises price and quantity; a rightward shift of supply lowers price and raises quantity. Equal shifts cancel the price effects but reinforce the rise in quantity.

stem: A government sets a minimum support price for wheat above the equilibrium price. The most likely result is
options: a fall in the price of wheat
explanation: A price floor above equilibrium makes farmers offer more and buyers take less, leaving unsold wheat. A floor set below equilibrium would have no effect, and a ceiling below equilibrium causes shortages.

stem: A fall in the price of petrol and, at the same time, a large rise in the number of car buyers would have what effect on the market for cars?
options: Demand for cars falls, lowering price and quantity
Only the quantity of cars changes, not price
Demand for cars rises, raising price and quantity
Supply of cars rises, lowering their price
explanation: Petrol is a complement to cars, so cheaper petrol raises car demand, and more buyers raise it further. Both factors shift the demand curve right, so with unchanged supply both price and quantity of cars rise.

stem: Price elasticity of demand measures the responsiveness of
options: quantity demanded to a change in consumers' money income
quantity demanded to a change in the good's price
supply to a change in the good's price
price to a change in quantity supplied
explanation: PED = % change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in price. Responsiveness of demand to income is income elasticity, and that of supply to price is elasticity of supply.

stem: The price of a packet of biscuits rises from Rs 50 to Rs 60 and the quantity demanded falls from 400 to 300 packets. Using the original values, what is the price elasticity of demand (in absolute terms)?
explanation: % change in quantity = 100 ÷ 400 = 25 %; % change in price = 10 ÷ 50 = 20 %. PED = 25 ÷ 20 = 1.25. 0.8 is the inverse ratio, price change over quantity change.

stem: When the price of a good falls by 10 %, its quantity demanded rises by 4 %. The demand for this good is
explanation: PED = 4 % ÷ 10 % = 0.4, which is less than 1, so demand is inelastic. 2.5 comes from dividing the price change by the quantity change.

stem: Demand for a good is price elastic. If its seller lowers the price, total revenue will
explanation: With elastic demand the percentage rise in quantity exceeds the percentage fall in price, so price × quantity rises. Revenue would fall only if demand were inelastic.

stem: A shopkeeper raises the price of salt and finds that his total revenue from salt rises. This shows that the demand for salt is
explanation: Under the total outlay method, revenue moving in the same direction as price means demand is inelastic: quantity falls proportionately less than price rises. Salt has few substitutes and takes a small share of income.

stem: When the price of a good falls from Rs 20 to Rs 15, total expenditure on it stays at Rs 3,000. The price elasticity of demand over this range is
explanation: Unchanged total expenditure after a price change is the sign of unitary elasticity in the total outlay method. Quantity rose from 150 to 200 exactly offsetting the lower price. Zero elasticity would mean quantity did not change at all, so spending would have fallen.

stem: A horizontal straight-line demand curve shows demand that is
explanation: A horizontal demand curve means buyers will take any quantity at one price but none above it: elasticity is infinite. A vertical curve shows perfectly inelastic demand.

stem: Which good is likely to have the most price-elastic demand?
options: One particular brand of soft drink
explanation: A single brand has many close substitutes, so buyers switch when its price rises. Salt, essential medicine and household electricity are necessities with few substitutes, so their demand is inelastic.

stem: Which factor makes the demand for a good more price inelastic?
options: Buyers have a long time to adjust
It takes a very small share of income
It is a luxury rather than a necessity
explanation: When spending on a good is a tiny part of the budget, a price change hardly matters to buyers, so demand is inelastic. More substitutes, luxury status and longer time to adjust all make demand more elastic.

stem: A consumer's income rises from Rs 40,000 to Rs 50,000 and her demand for fruit rises from 20 kg to 30 kg a month. Her income elasticity of demand for fruit is
explanation: % change in quantity = 10 ÷ 20 = 50 %; % change in income = 10,000 ÷ 40,000 = 25 %. YED = 50 ÷ 25 = 2. A positive value above 1 marks fruit as a luxury for her; 0.5 inverts the ratio.

stem: The income elasticity of demand for a good is negative. The good is
explanation: Negative income elasticity means demand falls as income rises, the definition of an inferior good. Necessities have income elasticity between 0 and 1, and luxuries above 1.

stem: The cross elasticity of demand between two goods is positive. The two goods are
explanation: A rise in the price of one good raising demand for the other gives a positive cross elasticity, the mark of substitutes such as tea and coffee. Complements have negative cross elasticity, and unrelated goods have zero.

stem: The price of good X rises by 20 % and the quantity demanded of good Y falls by 10 %. What is the cross elasticity of demand for Y with respect to the price of X, and how are the goods related?
explanation: Cross elasticity = % change in Qy ÷ % change in Px = −10 ÷ 20 = −0.5. The negative sign shows that dearer X reduces demand for Y, so they are used together. −2 comes from dividing the wrong way round.

stem: A vertical supply curve shows that the elasticity of supply is
explanation: A vertical supply curve means the same quantity is offered whatever the price, so quantity does not respond at all: elasticity is zero. Fresh fish at the end of a day's market is a common example.

stem: The price of a good rises from Rs 80 to Rs 100 and the quantity supplied rises from 500 to 600 units. Using the original values, the elasticity of supply is
explanation: % change in quantity supplied = 100 ÷ 500 = 20 %; % change in price = 20 ÷ 80 = 25 %. Es = 20 ÷ 25 = 0.8, so supply is inelastic. 1.25 is the inverse ratio.

stem: Supply of most farm crops is relatively inelastic in the short run mainly because
options: farmers do not respond to prices
output cannot be raised until the next harvest
demand for food is always elastic
crops are sold only by the government
explanation: Once a crop is sown, the quantity cannot be increased quickly; supply becomes more elastic over a longer period as farmers adjust what they plant. Farmers do respond to prices, but only with a time lag.

stem: In economics, utility means
options: the satisfaction a consumer gets from a good
the price a consumer pays for a good
the usefulness of a good to society
the cost of producing a good
explanation: Utility is the want-satisfying power of a good as felt by a consumer; it is subjective and need not be morally useful. A cigarette has utility for a smoker even though it harms health.

stem: The law of diminishing marginal utility states that as a consumer takes more units of a good,
options: the price of the good falls
total satisfaction falls from the first unit
the extra satisfaction from each unit rises
the extra satisfaction from each unit falls
explanation: Each additional unit adds less to total utility than the one before, because the want is gradually satisfied. Total utility still rises as long as marginal utility is positive.

stem: Hamza's total utility from eating 1, 2, 3 and 4 samosas is 20, 35, 45 and 50 utils respectively. What is the marginal utility of the third samosa?
explanation: MU of the third unit = TU(3) − TU(2) = 45 − 35 = 10 utils. 45 is the total utility of three samosas, and 15 is the MU of the second one.

stem: When marginal utility from a good is zero, total utility is
explanation: Total utility rises while MU is positive, stops rising when MU is zero and falls once MU turns negative. So zero MU marks the point of maximum total utility, the point of satiety.

stem: A consumer spends her income on goods X and Y. MU of X is 30 utils and its price is Rs 10; MU of Y is 40 utils and its price is Rs 20. To increase total utility she should
options: buy more Y and less X
buy more X and less Y
explanation: MUx ÷ Px = 30 ÷ 10 = 3 utils per rupee, and MUy ÷ Py = 40 ÷ 20 = 2. A rupee spent on X gives more satisfaction, so she should shift spending to X until the ratios are equal. Comparing MU alone wrongly points to Y.

stem: The law of equi-marginal utility says that a consumer gets maximum satisfaction from a given income when
options: MU per rupee is equal across all goods bought
the same amount is spent on each good
MU is equal for every good bought
total utility from each good is equal
explanation: Consumer equilibrium needs MUx ÷ Px = MUy ÷ Py = … for all goods, with all income spent. Equal MU without dividing by price ignores that goods cost different amounts.

stem: Consumer surplus is the difference between
options: what a consumer is willing to pay and what she actually pays
a consumer's income and her spending
the market price of a good and the seller's cost of production
explanation: Consumer surplus measures the extra benefit a buyer gets when the market price is below the most she would pay. The gap between price and cost relates to the producer's profit, not the consumer.

stem: Sana is willing to pay Rs 1,500 for a school bag but buys it for Rs 1,200. Her consumer surplus is
explanation: Consumer surplus = willingness to pay − price paid = 1,500 − 1,200 = Rs 300. Rs 1,200 is just the price she paid.

stem: A consumer is willing to pay Rs 50, Rs 40, Rs 30 and Rs 20 for the first, second, third and fourth units of a good. If the market price is Rs 20 and he buys 4 units, his total consumer surplus is
explanation: Surplus on each unit = willingness to pay − 20, giving 30 + 20 + 10 + 0 = Rs 60. Rs 140 is the total he is willing to pay, and Rs 80 is what he actually spends.

stem: An indifference curve shows combinations of two goods that give a consumer
options: the same quantity of each good
explanation: Every point on one indifference curve gives equal satisfaction, so the consumer is indifferent between them. Combinations costing the same lie on a budget line, not an indifference curve.

stem: Indifference curves are normally convex to the origin because of
options: a constant marginal rate of substitution
increasing marginal utility of both goods
a rise in the consumer's income
a diminishing marginal rate of substitution
explanation: As the consumer has more of X and less of Y, she gives up fewer and fewer units of Y for each extra unit of X; this falling MRS bends the curve towards the origin. A constant MRS would give a straight line, as with perfect substitutes.

stem: A consumer is in equilibrium on an indifference map at the point where
options: the budget line touches the highest indifference curve
the budget line cuts the lowest indifference curve
two indifference curves cross each other
the budget line meets the vertical axis
explanation: With a given income and prices, the best affordable combination is where the budget line is tangent to the highest reachable indifference curve, so MRS equals the price ratio. Indifference curves never cross.

stem: A consumer has Rs 600 to spend on good X at Rs 30 each and good Y at Rs 20 each. If she buys 10 units of X, how many units of Y can she buy with the rest?
explanation: Spending on X = 10 × 30 = Rs 300, leaving 600 − 300 = Rs 300 for Y. At Rs 20 each, she can buy 300 ÷ 20 = 15 units. 30 is the maximum Y if she bought no X.

stem: Goods that are freely available in nature and have no price, such as air, are called
explanation: Free goods are not scarce, so no sacrifice is needed to obtain them and they carry no price. Economic goods are scarce and command a price; public goods are non-rival and non-excludable but cost resources to provide.

stem: A demand schedule is a
options: table showing a firm's costs at each output
list of goods a household buys each month
graph showing quantities supplied at different prices
table showing quantities demanded at different prices
explanation: A demand schedule lists the price and the matching quantity demanded; plotting it gives the demand curve. A supply schedule does the same for quantities offered by sellers.

stem: Market demand for a good is obtained by
options: averaging the demand of all buyers
multiplying price by the quantity demanded
adding the quantities demanded by all buyers at each price
adding the prices that all buyers are willing to pay for one unit
explanation: Market demand is the horizontal sum of individual demand curves: at each price, add up what every buyer wants. Price × quantity gives expenditure, not market demand.

stem: Using the midpoint (arc) method, what is the price elasticity of demand when price rises from Rs 40 to Rs 60 and quantity demanded falls from 120 to 80 units?
explanation: Change in Q = 40 on an average of 100, so 40 %; change in P = 20 on an average of 50, so 40 %. PED = 40 ÷ 40 = 1. Using the starting values instead gives 33.3 % ÷ 50 % ≈ 0.67, which is why the midpoint method is used for large changes.

stem: On a straight-line downward-sloping demand curve, price elasticity of demand at the midpoint of the line is
options: the same as at every other point
explanation: Along a straight-line demand curve the slope is constant but elasticity is not: it is above 1 on the upper half, 1 at the midpoint and below 1 on the lower half. Equal slope does not mean equal elasticity.

stem: The phrase ceteris paribus, used when stating economic laws, means
options: only at the equilibrium market price
explanation: Laws such as the law of demand hold only if factors other than the one studied, such as income and tastes, do not change. It does not refer to time periods or market forms.

stem: Buyers expect the price of cement to rise sharply next month. The likely effect on the market for cement today is
options: demand falls and the demand curve shifts left
a movement down along the demand curve
supply rises and the supply curve shifts right
demand rises and the demand curve shifts right
explanation: Expecting higher future prices, buyers bring purchases forward, so demand at every current price increases. A movement along the curve would need a change in today's price, not in expectations.

stem: The demand for bricks that comes from the demand for new houses is an example of
explanation: Derived demand is demand for a good or factor because it helps produce something else that people want. Composite demand is when one good has several different uses, such as milk for butter and for tea.

stem: The government places a tax of Rs 10 per unit on a good whose demand is perfectly inelastic. Who bears the tax?
options: The sellers bear all of it
Buyers and sellers share it equally
The buyers bear all of it
explanation: With perfectly inelastic demand, buyers take the same quantity whatever the price, so sellers can pass the whole tax on and price rises by the full Rs 10. If demand were perfectly elastic, sellers would bear it all.

stem: The cardinal approach to utility assumes that utility
options: is the same for every consumer
can be measured in numbers called utils
is the same as the market price
can only be ranked in order of preference, not measured
explanation: Marshall's cardinal approach treats utility as measurable, so marginal utility can be stated as a number of utils. The ordinal, indifference curve approach only ranks combinations as preferred or indifferent.

stem: Demand for a good is Qd = 200 − 5P and supply is Qs = 50 + 10P. What is the equilibrium quantity?
explanation: Set 200 − 5P = 50 + 10P, so 150 = 15P and P = 10. Then Q = 200 − 50 = 150 units, and supply gives the same 50 + 100 = 150. 10 is the equilibrium price, not quantity.

stem: Which of these is a determinant of supply rather than of demand?
options: The state of technology used by firms
explanation: Technology changes the cost of production, so it shifts the supply curve. Tastes, population and income affect how much buyers want, so they shift demand.

stem: Wheat and straw are produced together, so they are in joint supply. If demand for wheat rises, the likely effect in the straw market is
options: demand for straw rises and its price rises
no change, as straw is a separate good
supply of straw falls and its price rises
supply of straw rises and its price falls
explanation: Growing more wheat automatically produces more straw, so the supply of straw shifts right and, with unchanged demand, its price falls. Treating straw as unrelated misses the link in production.

stem: At an output where price elasticity of demand equals one, a seller's total revenue is
explanation: While demand is elastic, a price cut raises revenue; once it becomes inelastic, a price cut lowers revenue. Revenue therefore peaks where elasticity is exactly one.

stem: An increase in demand, shown by a rightward shift of the demand curve, with supply unchanged leads to
options: a lower price and a larger quantity
a higher price and a smaller quantity
a higher price and a larger quantity
a lower price and a smaller quantity
explanation: At the old price there is now a shortage, so price rises and sellers move up the supply curve to offer more. A fall in price with a larger quantity is the result of an increase in supply.

stem: Which change would cause a contraction (fall in quantity) along the supply curve of mangoes?
options: A pest attack on mango orchards
A rise in the wages of farm workers
A new tax on each crate of mangoes
A fall in the market price of mangoes
explanation: Only a change in the good's own price moves sellers along the supply curve; a lower price leads them to offer less. Pests, higher wages and a per-unit tax raise costs or cut output at every price, shifting the curve left.
